Mundus — Technical Documentation
For Frontend & Backend Engineers
1. System Overview
Mundus is a verification platform for waste evacuation. It has three user types and one
core data object (the dump point) that everything else attaches to:
• Contractor supervisor (primary app user): logs before/after clearance photos at
assigned dump points.
• Agency (dashboard-only): views site status, never touches the field-facing app.
• Reporter (optional, per-site): a single designated person (shop owner, keke stage
operator) who can flag a site as full ahead of schedule.
There are no drivers as direct app users — see Section 3 for why.
2. Architecture
Suggested stack (optimized for an 18-day build, deployed on Pxxl):
• Frontend: React or Next.js (both supported natively on Pxxl)
• Backend: Node.js (Express or Fastify) — also natively supported on Pxxl, simplifies
having one deployment platform for both sides
• Database: PostgreSQL (or a managed Postgres instance if Pxxl doesn't provide one
— confirm what's available) or Firebase/Supabase if you want built-in auth and
storage to save build time
• File/photo storage: Object storage (S3-compatible, or Supabase Storage/Firebase
Storage) — do not store photos directly in the database
• Auth: Role-based — three roles (supervisor, agency-viewer, reporter), simplest
implemented via Supabase Auth or Firebase Auth with custom claims per role
Deployment (Pxxl):
• Frontend and backend both deploy via Pxxl's Git integration — push to a connected
GitHub repo, Pxxl handles CI/CD automatically.
• Use Pxxl's CLI (`pxxl auth`, then project-specific deploy commands) for manual
redeploys during the build sprint when you need faster iteration than git-push
triggers.
• Keep frontend and backend as separate Pxxl projects/services rather than one
monolith, so you can redeploy either independently without waiting on the other's
build.
• Use Pxxl's rollback feature as your safety net during the hackathon — if a late-stage
deploy breaks the demo, roll back rather than debug live.
Observability (WatchUp):
• Confirm with the organizers exactly what WatchUp tracks (uptime, error logging,
request tracing, or all three) before building your integration — treat the below as the
standard set to wire up regardless of which specific tool:
- Error tracking: wrap your backend API handlers so failed check-ins, failed photo
uploads, and failed geofence calculations are logged with enough context (site ID, user
ID, timestamp) to debug without needing to reproduce live during the demo.
- Uptime/health check endpoint: expose a simple `/health` route returning 200 OK,
since most observability tools poll this to confirm the service is alive — build this
early, it's a five-minute task that unblocks the whole integration.
- Basic request logging: log every check-in submission (success or failure) — this
doubles as an audit trail for your own demo prep, letting you show "here's every
check-in that happened during the build period" if asked.
3. Must-Have Features (MVP — build these first)
1 Dump point registry (admin-side). Create, list, and assign dump points to a
contractor. Minimal fields: name, coordinates, assigned contractor ID, assigned
supervisor ID.
2 Supervisor check-in flow.
- In-app camera capture only — no gallery/file upload. This is a hard requirement, not a
nice-to-have: it's your primary anti-fraud mechanism (see Section 5).
- Auto-capture GPS coordinates and timestamp at the moment the photo is taken —
read directly from device sensors, never a manual text field.
- Two capture types per visit: "before" and "after," tied to the same site + timestamp
pair.
1 Geofence validation. On submission, calculate the distance between the photo's
GPS coordinates and the registered dump point's coordinates (haversine formula — a
straightforward, well-documented calculation, no external library needed). If outside
a configurable radius (start with ~100m, adjust after testing), flag the submission as
"location mismatch" rather than silently accepting or rejecting it outright.
2 Agency dashboard — core view. A list of all registered dump points, each showing
days-since-last-clearance, sorted descending (most overdue first). Red-flag anything
past a configurable threshold (start with 10 days).
3 Fixed-interval scheduling logic. No cron job needed — compute "is this site
overdue" at read-time by comparing `now() - last_clearance_timestamp` against the
interval (e.g., 7 days) every time the dashboard loads. Simpler to build and demo
than a background job.
4 Basic auth with role separation. Supervisors can only see and act on their assigned
sites. Agency viewers see everything but can't submit check-ins. Keep this simple —
even a hardcoded role field checked on each request is fine for a hackathon MVP.
4. Nice-to-Have Features (build if time allows, after MVP is solid)
1 Reporter flow. Single-tap "site full" report from a designated reporter, tied to one
specific site. Feeds into the same overdue-ranking logic as an accelerant, not a
replacement.
2 Rate limiting on reporter submissions. Prevent the same site from being flagged
more than once per fixed window (e.g., once per 12 hours) — simple to implement
as a timestamp check before accepting a new report.
3 Timestamp sanity check. Flag (don't necessarily block) a submission where the
device timestamp seems inconsistent with server receipt time, as a secondary fraud
signal alongside the geofence check.
4 Before/after photo pairing view. A simple side-by-side view on the dashboard so
the agency can visually confirm a site was actually cleared, not just that two photos
were submitted.
5 Site-level history log. A timeline per dump point showing every check-in over time,
not just the current status — useful for a "look how consistent/inconsistent this
contractor has been" demo moment.
6 Push notifications. Real-time alert to a supervisor when a reporter flags their
assigned site, rather than requiring them to check the dashboard manually. Genuinely
buildable within the sprint, not a post-hackathon item — use Firebase Cloud
Messaging or Supabase's built-in realtime subscriptions (whichever matches your
auth/DB choice) rather than building push infrastructure from scratch. Budget a day
or two, not more.
7 Basic reused-photo detection. Hash each uploaded photo on submission (a standard
hashing function, no image-processing library needed) and check it against existing
hashes in the database. An exact match — the same file submitted for a different
check-in, or reused across sites — gets flagged automatically. This is a small,
well-scoped addition on top of the upload flow you're already building, not a
separate system. Distinct from photo *tamper* detection (see Section 7) — this only
catches identical files, not edited or visually similar ones.
5. Anti-Fraud & Anti-Spam — Technical Notes
• In-app camera only, no gallery upload is the single highest-leverage anti-fraud
measure and the easiest to implement — this alone prevents submitting an old photo
or a photo from a different location. On web, this means using `getUserMedia`
directly rather than a file input; on mobile, using the platform camera API directly
rather than an image picker.
• GPS-at-capture, not manual entry — read `navigator.geolocation` (web) or the
device's native location API (mobile) at the exact moment of capture, attach it to the
upload payload automatically. There is nothing for the user to type or fake here by
design.
• Geofence check happens server-side, not client-side — never trust a
client-reported "this photo is within range" flag; always recalculate distance on the
backend against the registered coordinates.
• Be upfront with your team (and in the demo) that GPS can still be spoofed by a
genuinely determined bad actor (mock location apps, rooted devices). The system
raises the cost of fraud and makes patterns detectable in aggregate — it does not
claim to be cryptographically tamper-proof. Don't oversell this part.
6. Explicitly Out of Scope for the Hackathon Build
• Offline support / sync-when-connected. Real engineering value, but too
time-costly for 18 days. Note it as a roadmap item.
• SMS-based reporting for non-smartphone users. Needs paid API setup (Twilio,
Africa's Talking) — not realistic alongside everything else. Name it as a future
accessibility improvement if asked.
• Real AKSEPWMA data or live contractor accounts. Everything is seeded demo
data — real dump point names, mock contractor/supervisor accounts you create
yourselves. Don't imply live government integration exists.
• Payment/payroll integration. Always framed as a policy recommendation for the
agency to adopt (see Edo State precedent), not something the software directly
executes.
7. Future Roadmap (post-hackathon, if this goes further)
1 Offline-first capture with background sync for low-connectivity areas.
2 SMS/USSD fallback reporting channel for non-smartphone reporters.
3 Multi-agency support — the same platform serving multiple LGAs or states (Abuja's
FCT has a documented, near-identical need).
4 Public-facing transparency dashboard (read-only, aggregated) for residents or
watchdog organizations — separate from the operational dashboard, and only after
the core product is proven with the agency.
5 Advanced photo-tamper detection beyond exact-duplicate hashing — perceptual
similarity matching and basic forensic checks to catch subtly edited or near-duplicate
images, not just identical reused files. Worth real engineering time once fraud
patterns are actually observed in production, not before.
8. Demo Data Checklist (for the live demo)
• 5–6 real dump point names and coordinates (Nwaniba, IBB Way, etc.)
• 2–3 mock contractor/supervisor accounts
• At least 2 sites deliberately left "overdue" to demonstrate the flagging logic working
live
• One full before/after check-in cycle walked through live, not pre-seeded, so the
judges see the actual flow
